questions.prompt: `OrdersService` injects `PricingService`, which is declared in `PricingModule`'s `providers`. Boot fails with "Nest can't resolve dependencies of the OrdersService (?)". What are the two things to check?

options.text: That `PricingModule` exports `PricingService`, and that `OrdersModule` imports `PricingModule`
Add `PricingService` to `OrdersModule`'s `providers` array
Mark `PricingService` as `@Global()`
That `OrdersController` is decorated with `@Injectable()`

questions.explanation: Modules are encapsulated: the injector searches this module's own providers plus the exports of its imports. So the provider must leave its home module (`exports`) and be let into yours (`imports`). Adding it to your own `providers` also "fixes" the error — by constructing a second, separate instance. `@Global()` is a module-level decorator, not a provider one.

questions.prompt: What is the actual consequence of listing the same service class in two modules' `providers` arrays?

options.text: Two independent instances — any in-memory state in one is invisible to the other
Nest throws a duplicate-provider error at boot
Nothing; Nest deduplicates by class and shares one instance
The last module to be loaded wins and the other injection is undefined

questions.explanation: `providers` means "instantiate this here". Each module gets its own instance, and the bug is silent until something stateful (a cache, a counter, an open connection, a subscription) diverges between them. One owner module + `exports` is the fix.

questions.prompt: `constructor(private mailer: Mailer)` where `Mailer` is a TypeScript `interface` fails to resolve. Why?

options.text: Interfaces don't exist at runtime, so there's no token for the injector to look up — use a string/symbol token with `@Inject`, or an abstract class
Interfaces can't be decorated with `@Injectable()`, so Nest skips them
It needs `strictPropertyInitialization` disabled in tsconfig
The parameter is missing `readonly`

questions.explanation: DI is driven by emitted metadata about the constructor's parameter types. A type that compiles away leaves `Object` behind, so there's nothing to resolve. `@Inject(MAILER)` with an exported `Symbol` (or an abstract class, which is both a type and a runtime value) gives you a real token.

questions.prompt: You need a Redis client whose URL comes from `ConfigService` and whose connection is established asynchronously. Which provider form?

options.text: `{ provide: "REDIS", useFactory: async (c: ConfigService) => …, inject: [ConfigService] }`
`{ provide: "REDIS", useClass: RedisClient }`
`{ provide: "REDIS", useValue: createClient(process.env.REDIS_URL) }`
Connect inside the consuming service's constructor

questions.explanation: Of the four forms, `useFactory` is the only one that can both await setup and depend on other providers (via the positional `inject` array). `useValue` would run the connect at module-load time, outside Nest's control and untestable; connecting in a constructor makes construction slow and un-awaitable. The other legitimate shape is a `useClass` provider that connects in `onModuleInit` — Nest awaits that hook — which is what you want when the connection has a lifecycle (reconnects, graceful shutdown) rather than being a one-shot value.

questions.prompt: A service stores `this.currentUser` at the start of each request and reads it later in the call. What's the failure mode?

options.text: Providers are app-wide singletons, so concurrent requests overwrite each other's `currentUser`
The field is garbage collected between the await points
None — Nest creates a provider per request by default
Only a typing problem, since the field must be optional

questions.explanation: `Scope.DEFAULT` is one instance for the whole application. Any "current request" field is shared mutable state across concurrent requests, and it fails intermittently under load — the worst kind of bug. Pass the value as an argument, or use `AsyncLocalStorage`; `Scope.REQUEST` works but spreads per-request instantiation up the whole injection chain.

questions.prompt: What do you give up by marking many modules `@Global()`?

options.text: The module graph stops documenting real dependencies — nothing declares what it needs, so coupling and boot-order problems become invisible
Global providers are no longer singletons
Global modules can't be overridden in `Test.createTestingModule`
Resolution becomes O(n) at request time

questions.explanation: `@Global()` is a legitimate tool for root infrastructure registered once (config, logger, DB connection). Used broadly it removes the `imports` lines that were your dependency documentation, and "who can reach this?" becomes "everyone". Globals are still singletons and still overridable in tests.

prompts.prompt: Let another module inject `OrdersService` while keeping `OrdersRepository` private to this module.
prompts.explanation: `exports` is the module's public API. `OrdersRepository` stays out of it, so it remains an implementation detail — and only one instance of each exists, because they're constructed exactly once here.

prompts.prompt: Inject an implementation behind an interface, using an explicit symbol token.
prompts.explanation: `@Inject(token)` overrides the metadata-based lookup, which is what makes interface-typed dependencies possible. The module then registers `{ provide: MAILER, useClass: SesMailer }` — and a test registers `{ provide: MAILER, useValue: fake }` in the same slot.

prompts.prompt: Build a provider asynchronously from another provider.
prompts.explanation: `useFactory` may be async — Nest awaits it during boot, which is why the factory can return an already-connected client — and `inject` supplies its parameters positionally. Swap the factory's body and every consumer is unaffected: they depend on the token, not on how it's built.

prompts.prompt: Replace a real dependency with a fake in a unit test, using the same token the injector uses.
prompts.explanation: This is DI's payoff: no module mocking, no import interception — you register a different value under the same token. `useValue` takes any object that satisfies the shape the consumer actually calls.

snippets.question: What do the three calls return?
snippets.explanation: One instance per application, shared by both controllers — so the counter keeps climbing across requests and across consumers. That's exactly why an instance field is fine for a cache and catastrophic for "the current user".

snippets.question: What does BService read back?
snippets.explanation: Listing `CacheService` in both `providers` arrays constructs it twice, so each module holds its own `Map`. Nest boots without complaint. One owner module + `exports` + `imports` is the only way to share the instance.

snippets.question: What does onModuleInit log, and why is the constructor version unsafe?
acceptable: init: false — the connect promise wasn't awaited
snippets.explanation: A constructor can't be awaited, so the un-awaited `connect()` is still pending when Nest continues booting — the app can start serving before the dependency is usable. Async setup belongs in `onModuleInit` (which Nest awaits) or in a `useFactory`.
